A few words first

For a long time I have followed the acoustics blog of Trevor Cox, a professor at the University of Salford in the UK. In fact, he is part of the reason I started writing popular science myself. Cox works mainly on architectural acoustics and has co-written a book on sound absorbers and diffusers [1]. But what made his name was not that book. It was his two popular-science books, Sonic Wonderland and Now You’re Talking, and his blog, which have drawn the attention of the BBC, The Guardian and other media.

I was recently lucky enough to get in touch with Professor Cox, and we discussed how to bring his blog and his popular acoustics to readers in China. Over the coming months we will publish a series of articles based on his work on our WeChat account, Ziyu Acoustics, combining his blog posts with my own understanding and additions. The focus will be on the human voice, speech and audio. These topics are closer to everyday life and suit a general audience better, and it is the first time I have tried this kind of article. I hope you enjoy it, and that we all learn something along the way.

For the first article in the series, I want to talk about the “uncanny valley” of sound.

The uncanny valley

The uncanny valley was proposed in 1970 by the Japanese roboticist Masahiro Mori. It describes the intense discomfort we feel when a robot looks very human but has some odd feature or other. Say, a face that is entirely human except for eyes that are much too big… Yes, the classic example is the kind of photo we all know from WeChat Moments, China’s social media feed, where beauty filters run wild.

Some people also complained that Alita’s oversized eyes in Alita: Battle Angel were unsettling to look at.

And a while ago, a zombie-like sloth gave people a fright.

It’s precisely when something is fairly human that it gives us that creepy “human, yet not human” feeling.

Wikipedia explains the uncanny valley like this:

Mori’s hypothesis states that as a robot becomes more humanlike in appearance and motion, people’s emotional response to it becomes increasingly positive, until a certain point is reached, beyond which the response suddenly turns strongly negative. Even a tiny difference between the robot and a human then becomes glaring, and the whole robot seems stiff and eerie, like facing a zombie. But as the robot’s resemblance to humans keeps increasing, to the level of resemblance between ordinary people, the emotional response becomes positive again, approaching human-to-human empathy.

In short, a robot that looks very human, or not very human, causes no discomfort. It only falls into the uncanny valley when it is fairly human but still noticeably different, like the puppets, prostheses, corpses and zombies mentioned in the figure below. The future robot beauties of Westworld (the most… →_→) don’t count, because they are played by real actors…

From left to right: an industrial robot arm; the puppet from Saw; the robot Sophia; the robot Dolores from Westworld

An uncanny valley for voices?

Since the uncanny valley concerns how visually similar a man-made machine is to a human, its counterpart in sound would be the relationship between synthesized human voices and real ones. So wherever I mention sound below, I mean the human voice.

Back to the question, then: can the human voice produce an uncanny valley effect? For example when a person’s image and voice appear together but the face moves slightly out of sync with the voice, or when a robot’s voice sounds too much like a human’s [2, 3]. Take Repliee Q2, one of the many humanoid robots built by the ever-inventive Japanese. To be honest, it is already very creepy without a voice, let alone with one. Imagine sitting on the sofa with her in the evening, watching TV and chatting. Couldn’t be cozier!

The Repliee Q2 robot

But what about the voice on its own?

If a recording of speech doesn’t sound human, we simply file it as synthetic. We won’t mistake it for a human voice, let alone find it frightening. Telephones, radio, WeChat voice messages and other media all alter the voice, and they have long since made us immune to just about every variation of it, to say nothing of the sound effects in films.

Also from Japan, a singing robot appeared in 2008. Its main purpose was to help hearing-impaired people learn to vocalize correctly by simulating the mechanism of human voice production [4]. Viewer discretion advised: the video below may be unsettling. But close your eyes and listen, and apart from the racket, there is nothing scary about it.

The singing robot

Some have pointed to the distortions of sound-field reproduction in virtual reality [5]. With headphone playback, for instance, sources can seem to sit inside your head; or, going by experience, the scene you see doesn’t match the sound field you hear. But all this only makes things feel unreal. It doesn’t make them frightening.

Everything seems to lead to a rather unexciting conclusion: an uncanny valley for the human voice may not exist at all. If it did, wouldn’t Hollywood’s sound designers have found it long ago?

What do you think about an uncanny valley for voices? If you have had a similar experience, in real life or in your imagination, leave a comment! Let me hear your voices!

References

Source of the topic:

https://acousticengineering.wordpress.com/2019/04/21/the-uncanny-valley-does-it-happen-with-voices/

1. Cox, T., & D’Antonio, P. (2016). Acoustic absorbers and diffusers: theory, design and application. CRC Press.

2. Tinwell, A., Grimshaw, M. and Nabi, D. A., 2015. ‘The effect of onset asynchrony in audio-visual speech and the Uncanny Valley in virtual characters’. International Journal of Mechanisms and Robotic Systems, 2(2), pp. 97–110.

3. Mitchell, W. J., Szerszen Sr, K. A., Lu, A. S., Schermerhorn, P. W., Scheutz, M. and MacDorman, K. F., 2011. ‘A mismatch in the human realism of face and voice produces an uncanny valley’. i-Perception, 2(1), pp. 10–12.

4. Sawada, H., Kitani, M., & Hayashi, Y. (2008). A robotic voice simulator and the interactive training for hearing-impaired people. BioMed Research International, 2008.

5. https://www.inverse.com/article/5365-virtual-reality-lost-uncanny-valley-sound
